steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our numeric planning paper that introduces symbolic pattern planning, a new encoding for solving numeric planning problems symbolically. Give the background on numeric planning, explain the idea and its advantages over earlier encodings, summarize the experiments, and outline the rest of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Background: numeric planning and current solving approaches
- Contribution: symbolic pattern planning and the pattern encoding
- Experimental evaluation and the planner Patty
- Paper structure

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - planning: one of oldest AI problems
  - classical: all variables Boolean
  - simple numeric: variables over rationals; actions increment/decrement by fixed constant
  - linear numeric: actions can set variable to linear combination of values in the current state
  - approaches for numeric problem \Pi: search-based (heuristic search over state space) vs symbolic-based (fix bound n a priori, encode plan-with-bound-n as formula with a decision procedure)
- Contribution: symbolic pattern planning
  - given \Pi and pattern {\prec} (sequence of actions)
  - generalize rolled-up encoding \Pi^{R} and relaxed-relaxed- \exists ({R^{2}\exists}{}) encoding \Pi^{R^{2}\exists}{}
  - new encoding \Pi^{\prec} provably dominates both: for any bound n, never the case they find a valid plan and ours doesn't
  - fewer clauses than rolled-up, far fewer variables than R^{2}\exists, even at fixed bound
  - new starting point for symbolic approaches: pattern = any action sequence (even with repetitions)
  - with n=1, formula encodes all sequences where each action in {\prec} executed zero, one or more times
  - any problem solvable with n=1 given a suitable pattern; pattern can be searched symbolically / defined incrementally while increasing the bound -> bridges symbolic and search-based planning
- Experiments
  - (i) 2 planners, benchmarks, settings of just concluded IPC, Agile track
  - (ii) 4 more planning systems, simple and linear numeric
  - total 6 other planners: 3 symbolic, 3 search-based
  - Patty always better than other symbolic planners on every domain
  - vs all planners: remarkably good overall, fastest system solving most problems on largest number of domains
- Structure
  - preliminaries; rolled-up, R^{2}\exists, pattern encodings + dominance proof; experiments; conclusion
  - one running example throughout for definitions and results

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Planning is one of the oldest problems in Artificial Intelligence. In the classical setting all the variables are Boolean. In simple numeric planning problems the variables can also range over the rationals, and actions can increment or decrement their values by a fixed constant. In linear numeric planning problems actions can also update variables to a new value that is a linear combination of the values of the variables in the state where the actions are executed. The current approaches for solving a numeric planning problem \Pi are either search-based, where the state space is explored with techniques based on heuristic search, or symbolic-based, where a bound n on the number of steps is fixed a priori and the problem of finding a plan with bound n is encoded into a formula for which a decision procedure is available.

In this paper we propose a new symbolic approach for solving numeric planning problems, which we call symbolic pattern planning. Given a problem \Pi and a pattern {\prec}, which is a sequence of actions, we show how to generalize the state-of-the-art rolled-up encoding \Pi^{R} proposed in earlier work and the relaxed-relaxed- \exists ({R^{2}\exists}{}) encoding \Pi^{R^{2}\exists}{} proposed in other work, and we define a new encoding \Pi^{\prec} which provably dominates both \Pi^{R} and \Pi^{R^{2}\exists}{}. This means that for any bound n, it never happens that the latter two find a valid plan for \Pi and ours does not. Also, our encoding produces formulas with fewer clauses than the rolled-up encoding and with far fewer variables than the R^{2}\exists encoding, even with a fixed bound. Most importantly, we think our proposal is a new starting point for symbolic approaches. A pattern {\prec} can be any sequence of actions (even with repetitions), and if n=1, the formula produced by \Pi^{\prec} encodes all the sequences of actions in which each action in {\prec} is executed sequentially zero, one or possibly more than one time. So any planning problem can be solved with bound n=1 if a suitable pattern is used, and such a pattern can be searched symbolically and defined incrementally also while the bound increases, which bridges the gap between symbolic and search-based planning.

- Experiments
  - (i) 2 planners, benchmarks, settings of just concluded IPC, Agile track
  - (ii) 4 more planning systems, simple and linear numeric
  - total 6 other planners: 3 symbolic, 3 search-based
  - Patty always better than other symbolic planners on every domain; fastest system solving most problems on largest number of domains
- Structure
  - preliminaries; encodings + dominance proof; experiments; conclusion
  - one running example throughout

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Planning is one of the oldest problems in Artificial Intelligence. In the classical setting all the variables are Boolean. In simple numeric planning problems the variables can also range over the rationals, and actions can increment or decrement their values by a fixed constant. In linear numeric planning problems actions can also update variables to a new value that is a linear combination of the values of the variables in the state where the actions are executed. The current approaches for solving a numeric planning problem \Pi are either search-based, where the state space is explored with techniques based on heuristic search, or symbolic-based, where a bound n on the number of steps is fixed a priori and the problem of finding a plan with bound n is encoded into a formula for which a decision procedure is available.

In this paper we propose a new symbolic approach for solving numeric planning problems, which we call symbolic pattern planning. Given a problem \Pi and a pattern {\prec}, which is a sequence of actions, we show how to generalize the state-of-the-art rolled-up encoding \Pi^{R} proposed in earlier work and the relaxed-relaxed- \exists ({R^{2}\exists}{}) encoding \Pi^{R^{2}\exists}{} proposed in other work, and we define a new encoding \Pi^{\prec} which provably dominates both \Pi^{R} and \Pi^{R^{2}\exists}{}. This means that for any bound n, it never happens that the latter two find a valid plan for \Pi and ours does not. Also, our encoding produces formulas with fewer clauses than the rolled-up encoding and with far fewer variables than the R^{2}\exists encoding, even with a fixed bound. Most importantly, we think our proposal is a new starting point for symbolic approaches. A pattern {\prec} can be any sequence of actions (even with repetitions), and if n=1, the formula produced by \Pi^{\prec} encodes all the sequences of actions in which each action in {\prec} is executed sequentially zero, one or possibly more than one time. So any planning problem can be solved with bound n=1 if a suitable pattern is used, and such a pattern can be searched symbolically and defined incrementally also while the bound increases, which bridges the gap between symbolic and search-based planning.

To show that our proposal is effective, we (i) considered the 2 planners, the benchmarks, and the settings of the IPC, Agile track, which just concluded; and (ii) added 4 more planning systems for both simple and linear numeric problems. So in total our comparison included 6 other planners, 3 symbolic and 3 search-based. The results show that our planner Patty always performs better than the other symbolic planners on every domain. Compared to all the other planners, Patty has overall remarkably good performance, and it is the fastest system able to solve most problems on the largest number of domains.

The paper is structured as follows. After the preliminaries we present the rolled-up, R^{2}\exists and pattern encodings, and we prove that our encoding dominates the other two. Then come the experimental analysis and the conclusion. We use one running example throughout the paper to illustrate the formal definitions and the theoretical results.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Planning is one of the oldest problems in Artificial Intelligence, see, e.g., [1]. Starting from the classical setting in which all the variables are Boolean, in simple numeric planning problems variables can also range over the rationals and actions can increment or decrement their values by a fixed constant, while in linear numeric planning problems actions can also update variables to a new value which is a linear combination of the values of the variables in the state in which actions are executed, see, e.g., [2]. Current approaches for solving a numeric planning problem \Pi are either search-based (where the state space is explored using techniques based on heuristic search, see, e.g., [3]) or symbolic-based (where a bound n on the number of steps is fixed a priori and the problem of finding a plan with bound n is encoded into a formula for which a decision procedure is available, see, e.g., [4]).

In this paper, we propose a novel symbolic approach for solving numeric planning problems, called symbolic pattern planning. Given a problem \Pi and a pattern {\prec} – defined as a sequence of actions – we show how to generalize the state-of-the-art rolled-up encoding \Pi^{R} proposed in [5] and the relaxed-relaxed- \exists ({R^{2}\exists}{}) encoding \Pi^{R^{2}\exists}{} proposed in [6], and define a new encoding \Pi^{\prec} which provably dominates both \Pi^{R} and \Pi^{R^{2}\exists}{}: for any bound n, it is never the case that the latter two find a valid plan for \Pi while ours does not. Further, our encoding produces formulas with fewer clauses than the rolled-up encoding and with far fewer variables than the R^{2}\exists encoding, even with a fixed bound. Most importantly, we believe our proposal provides a new starting point for symbolic approaches: a pattern {\prec} can be any sequence of actions (even with repetitions) and, assuming n=1, the formula produced by \Pi^{\prec} encodes all the sequences of actions in which each action in {\prec} is sequentially executed zero, one or possibly more than one time. Thus, any planning problem can be solved with bound n=1 given a suitable pattern, and such a pattern can be symbolically searched and incrementally defined also while increasing the bound, bridging the gap between symbolic and search-based planning.

To show the effectiveness of our proposal, we (i) considered the 2 planners, benchmarks, and settings of the just concluded IPC, Agile track [2]; and (ii) added 4 other planning systems for both simple and linear numeric problems. Overall, our comparison included 6 other planners, 3 symbolic and 3 search-based. The results show that our planner Patty always performs better than the other symbolic planners on every domain, while compared to all the other planners, Patty has overall remarkably good performance, being the fastest system able to solve most problems on the largest number of domains.

The paper is structured as follows. After the preliminaries, we present the rolled-up, R^{2}\exists and our pattern encodings, and prove that the latter dominates the other two. The experimental analysis and the conclusion then follow. A single running example is used throughout the paper to illustrate the formal definitions and the theoretical results.

References:
